title: Formal parameter
body:
The variables named in a [[Function]]'s **prototype and definition**. They are the names the
function uses for its inputs, and they exist only inside the function.

```c++
void my_function(int formal_parameter);      // declaration

void my_function(int formal_parameter) {     // definition
	cout << formal_parameter;                // used by name in here
}
```

The counterpart is the [[Actual parameter]], which is what the caller actually hands over at
the call site. Formal is the placeholder, actual is the value that fills it.

Formal parameters are ordinary local variables as far as [[Variable Scope]] and
[[Variable Lifetime]] are concerned: they come into existence when the function is entered and
vanish when it returns. Which is exactly why [[Call by value]] cannot change the caller's
variable, and why `int&` ([[Call by reference]]) is needed when it must.

The names do not have to match the caller's, and usually should not. `my_function(count)` binds
`count` to `formal_parameter` by **position**, not by name. Get the order wrong and you have a
[[Logic Errors|logic error]] the compiler will not catch, as long as the types line up.
